items.fact: HumanEval (2021, Codex paper): 164 hand-written Python functions from docstrings
HumanEval: pass@k via unit tests
HumanEval: origin of the unbiased pass@k estimator (the Math page uses the estimator in its Sample lab and cites the Codex paper; the definition and history belong to Coding)
HumanEval: saturated (>99%) and retired
MBPP (974 basic problems): same story
EvalPlus / HumanEval+ hardened the test suites (80x more tests) and knocked several points off inflated scores
Lesson: weak test suites overstate correctness, recurring in every code benchmark since
BigCodeBench (2024): library-heavy, multi-call tasks; saturating
LiveCodeBench (2024): continuously harvests new problems from LeetCode, AtCoder and Codeforces with release dates attached
LiveCodeBench: any model can be evaluated on post-cutoff problems only, contamination control by construction
LiveCodeBench: also tests self-repair, test-output prediction and execution
LiveCodeBench: frontier models ~90% on recent windows
LiveCodeBench Pro (2025): Olympiad/ICPC-grade problems annotated by medalists
LiveCodeBench Pro: Elo-style rating against the human distribution rather than pass@1
LiveCodeBench Pro: frontier ratings ~2800-2900 in mid-2026 (grandmaster-plus), still failing observation-heavy insight problems
Labs report Codeforces ratings from live or simulated contest runs; o3 ~2700 was the 2024 headline
2026 frontier models claim Codeforces 3000+, top-tens-of-humans territory
IOI and ICPC live runs (gold-medal results in 2025/26) serve the 'no contamination possible' claim (the Math page covers the IMO counterpart)
SWE-bench (2023, Princeton): 2,294 real GitHub issues from 12 Python repos
SWE-bench: repo at the pre-fix commit plus issue text, model must produce a patch, scored by the repo's own fail-to-pass tests
SWE-bench turned code evals from function completion into repo-level engineering; de facto coding-agent benchmark
Lite (300): cheaper subset, popular 2024, now rarely reported
Verified (500, 2024): OpenAI paid engineers to filter broken tasks (underspecified issues, unfair tests; ~33% of the original had problems)
Verified: the standard 2024-25 number
Verified: Aug 2026 SOTA ~97% (Claude Opus 5-class), effectively saturated
Verified known issues: solution leakage in issue comments, weak test suites, repo-memorization (worse on repos created after cutoff, per SWE-bench-Illusion and SWE-rebench)
Pro (2025, Scale): 1,865 tasks from 41 repos
Pro: copyleft-licensed and private commercial repos as a contamination guard; human-augmented problem statements; multi-file reference fixes
Pro: public-split SOTA ~59% (Scale harness), vendor-scaffold ~80%, private commercial split ~47%; scaffold and split swing a SOTA claim by 30 points
Multimodal (2024): JavaScript repos with screenshots/visual bug reports
SWE-rebench / SWE-bench-Live: continuously mined fresh issues, monthly updates, decontaminated by recency; cited as the honest alternative
Real-SWE (2026, Specific Labs): ten tasks licensed from real companies' production repositories, median 11 files changed per task
Real-SWE: each model in its native harness over 640 scored rollouts

Real-SWE Sep 2026 scores: Fable 5.1 38.8%, GPT-6 Astra 33.8%, Gemini 3.8 Flash 31.2%, GLM-5.3 28.8%, Grok 4.6 and Muse Spark 1.3 23.8%, Kimi K3 18.8%, GPT-5.6 Sol 16.2% (atlas correction: board now Astra 46.25%, Fable 5.1 45.0%)
Real-SWE: six of ten tasks resolved under 15%; missed requirements the commonest failure
Real-SWE: 71.4% of rollouts finishing in under ten minutes failed
Real-SWE: cost per rollout ($2.50 to $6.96) had no relationship to score
Real-SWE: against the same models' Terminal-Bench 4.0 figures, private code costs roughly 20 points
Real-SWE: licensing as the methodological contribution, the only contamination defence not depending on novelty; resource link withspecific.com/benchmarks/real-swe (15 min)
Metric subtlety: % resolved conflates model and agent harness (scaffold, retries, test execution, compute budget)
Leaderboards mark open scaffold vs bash-only vs proprietary; never compare across those columns
SWE-bench counts as an agentic benchmark; link to the Agentic benchmarks page (3c65c17b0d0d811fb926d7b91ef8234e)
Aider Polyglot (2024): 225 hard Exercism problems across 6 languages in an edit-format harness
Aider Polyglot: practitioner-favored, correlates with coding-assistant usefulness, cheap to run
Phi-Bench (2026): infrastructure engineering, 85 open-ended tasks in nine categories (training systems, inference and serving, kernels, hardware adaptation, data infrastructure, others)
Phi-Bench: three formats, 55 single-file kernel completions, 20 multi-file repository implementations, 10 end-to-end optimisations
Phi-Bench: built from PR/issue reconstruction, agent-assisted mining with generated tests, and expert curation; grounded in 2,260 papers and 1,852 engineering artifacts

Phi-Bench: Claude Opus 5 36.53%, Kimi K3 28.12%, Qwen3.8-Max 27.73%; hardware and edge tasks collapse to 5.4%; longer reasoning budgets do not reliably help; summary page 3db5c17b0d0d81029236da6c38f5891f
Model-level codegen: LiveCodeBench (latest window) plus LiveCodeBench Pro rating

Agentic engineering: SWE-bench Pro (state split and scaffold), Terminal-Bench 4.0 (current since Sep 2026; 2.x not comparable), Real-SWE for a private-code check; SWE-bench Verified only for continuity
Math: current-year AIME/HMMT via the MathArena protocol, FrontierMath tiers for frontier claims
